You are a research assistant answering questions about a fixed set of papers.
The papers are plain-text files in your working directory. Explore them with the tools:
- bash: read-only shell (ls, grep -n, find, head, tail, wc, nl, cat, sed -n 'A,Bp')
- read(path, offset, limit): read a file with line numbers

Rules:
- Answer ONLY from text you have actually read in this session. Do not answer from memory.
- If the papers do not contain the answer, say so explicitly instead of guessing.
- When you have enough evidence, reply with your final answer and make NO tool call.
- Support every factual claim with a verbatim quote copied exactly from the source, in the form: "exact text" (file). Never paraphrase inside the quotation marks. A statement that the document(s) do not contain the requested information needs no citation.
- State only what the document(s) say. Do not add background knowledge, general advice, or your own
  conclusions. If the user asks for something the text only partly covers, answer the covered part
  and say plainly which part the document does not address.
- Do not expand abbreviations, name entities, or add details that the text itself does not give.
- Do not end with a summary that recombines earlier points ("In short", "Overall"); the points stand on their own.
- When the user describes their own situation, say what the document states that applies to it; do not
  draw a personal conclusion that the document does not state itself.
- After you give an answer, an automatic check verifies your citations. If you then receive a
  <verification> message, you are in revision mode: fix ONLY the flagged problems by calling
  edit_draft(old, new), where `old` is an exact, unique substring of your previous answer.
  Keep everything else unchanged, and reply "Done" when finished.
  Never call edit_draft before you have given an answer.

What are the arguments for and against the Bill?

In your answer, refer only to the document in the file `doc.txt`. Do not employ any outside knowledge.

name: read
content:
1	The new British Ambassador to the United States, prior to his departure for Washington, perhaps with
     2	the idea of propitiating Irish opinion in America, elected to speak on St. Patrick's Day. He wore a
     3	green Irish halo for the occasion. He said it had been a labor of love for him during last summer
     4	and autumn to assist in reducing to legislative form proposals for ending the Irish question. He
     5	said the new Bill for the government of Ireland was "a sincere attempt to place definitely and
     6	finally in the hands of the elected representatives of the Irish people the duty and responsibility
     7	of working out their own salvation and the salvation of their country." No doubt this statement has
     8	been cabled to America, and I propose to examine here how far this statement is justified and how
     9	Ireland is indebted to Sir Auckland Geddes for his interest in its welfare. I lay this down as a
    10	fundamental proposition, which I do not think will be denied, that whoever controls the taxation and
    11	trade policy of a country controls its destiny and the entire character of its civilization. The
    12	body with control over customs, excise, income tax, supertax, excess profits duty and external trade
    13	has it in its power to make that country predominantly industrial or agricultural or to make a
    14	balance between urban and rural interests. It can direct the external trade of the country, make it
    15	flow into this or that channel. These powers over Irish taxation and trade policy are expressly
    16	denied to Ireland. Ireland in fact has less power under this last Bill over its own economic
    17	development than it had under the Act of Union. Under that Act, Ireland had one hundred and two
    18	members in the Imperial Parliament who could at times hold the balance of power. It was not a very
    19	real power, because when the interests of Ireland and Great Britain conflicted, both parties in
    20	Great Britain united against Ireland, but still to the leaders of parties Irish votes were worth
    21	angling for, for British purposes, and had to be paid for by Land Acts or other measures. The new
    22	Bill provides that the Irish representation at Westminster shall be reduced to forty-two members,
    23	and so at Westminster Ireland is made practically powerless, while everything which really affects
    24	Irish economic interests is still legislated for by the British Parliament.

**Argument for the Bill**

The only favorable statement in the document is that of the new British Ambassador to the United States, who said the new Bill for the government of Ireland was "a sincere attempt to place definitely and finally in the hands of the elected representatives of the Irish people the duty and responsibility of working out their own salvation and the salvation of their country." **Arguments against the Bill**

The author of the document rejects the Ambassador's statement and argues as follows:

2. The Bill withholds these powers from Ireland: "These powers over Irish taxation and trade policy are expressly denied to Ireland." (doc.txt) The body controlling "customs, excise, income tax, supertax, excess profits duty and external trade" can make a country "predominantly industrial or agricultural" and "direct the external trade of the country," yet Ireland is denied these powers. (doc.txt)

3. The Bill gives Ireland less power than the Act of Union: "Ireland in fact has less power under this last Bill over its own economic development than it had under the Act of Union." (doc.txt) Under the Act of Union, Ireland had "one hundred and two members in the Imperial Parliament who could at times hold the balance of power," and "to the leaders of parties Irish votes were worth angling for, for British purposes, and had to be paid for by Land Acts or other measures." (doc.txt)

4. The Bill reduces Irish representation and leaves economic legislation to Britain: "The new Bill provides that the Irish representation at Westminster shall be reduced to forty-two members, and so at Westminster Ireland is made practically powerless, while everything which really affects Irish economic interests is still legislated for by the British Parliament." (doc.txt)

The document does not present any further arguments in favor of the Bill beyond the Ambassador's statement, which the author sets out to examine "how far this statement is justified." (doc.txt)
